ops.markdown:
**Wanderline** is a travel company; Farah is its CEO and founder. Carried over from last class.

**The business problem.** Enquiries arrive at three or four in the morning. Nobody acts on them. Clients are being lost.

An enquiry arriving at 3am does not need anyone's judgement at 3am — it needs someone to have seen it by 9am. That is what makes it automatable rather than a staffing problem.

**Why today looks different from last class.** Last class showed workflows but did not implement anything that responds to the client — a showcase, not a use case. Today is three iterated builds against one real scenario.

**Today's first goal**

> Whenever a new request comes in, consolidate it and email a summary to the team.

That sentence is Build 1's entire spec, and it reads straight onto the three-node starting rule: *whenever a new request comes in* is the input, *consolidate it* is the AI step, *email a summary* is somewhere to put the result.

Traps collected as they came up across the lecture.

**A workflow that is built but not published never triggers automatically.** Nothing errors and nothing is red — the canvas looks finished, the nodes are configured, testing works. To trigger automatically the workflow must be published and the publish button actually green.

ops.title: Build 1 — form to LLM chain to Gmail

ops.label: n8n Form trigger
ops.detail: Form title "Wanderline late-night inquiries", no authentication. Exposes a test URL and a production URL — sandbox for your own changes versus what clients see. Run Execute step and submit once, so the next node is configured against real sample data rather than guesses.

ops.label: Basic LLM Chain, with a Groq model sub-node
ops.detail: Source for prompt: define below, not the chat trigger. Prompt: "Summarize this travel inquiry in two short lines for our team inbox. In case of vague description you can clean and refine the text." The form's name and query are dragged in from the input panel, which converts each to an expression; the preview at the bottom shows the resolved prompt with the real values substituted.

ops.label: Gmail — send a message
ops.detail: To himself, subject "New request, please check", body = the chain's text output picked from the schema view, plus a sign-off. Credentials: OAuth every time when it is your own account; the API key route (enable the Gmail API in Google Cloud, create a project and key, free) is for when someone hands you a key for an account you are not logged into.

ops.label: It cannot tell a spam request from a real one
ops.detail: A query about grocery prices at the local market — nothing to do with travel — was summarised and emailed anyway. No spam detection means the inbox is overburdened and the person reading it drowns. The build is not broken: it does exactly what the goal sentence asked. The goal sentence was incomplete, and only a real submission showed that. This is what Build 2 answers.

cells.c-why: Someone will type +91 and a number field rejects it. Pick the field type by what people will actually enter, not by what the data nominally is
A text input caps out and silently truncates; a textarea expands and holds a long query. A travel enquiry is prose
Added mid-build after a student pointed out they were missing — the flow was already running when the gap surfaced
Nothing was mandatory on the first run: submitting with no email was accepted with no nudge. Set per element under Add an attribute

cells.c-verdict: Could be stable, but nowhere close to the frontier assistants
Would potentially work fine on a laptop through Ollama
Going to fail for sure on a laptop
Impossible even with two or three high-end NVIDIA cards
A simple request does not need an expensive model. Summarisation is simple — any model can do it

Check the cut-off date. A model with a 2023 cut-off is fine for English summarisation or general coding and useless on anything newer. There is no single reliable page for cut-offs — ask the model, or check the Ollama model pages
The small model picked here starts hallucinating in Build 3. "Simple task" is a judgement you can get wrong, and the symptom surfaces two builds later
Deliberately not recorded — every model name in the lecture is machine-heard and unverified. The thresholds are the lesson, not the labels

ops.markdown:
**Change the trigger, re-run the trigger.** Sample data is a snapshot of the last successful execution, not a live connection. Editing the form after submitting makes the earlier submission stale, and the node downstream summarises nothing.

**Drag the leaf, not the parent — and use schema view, not table view.** Schema view is the tree of an upstream node's output, so it is the only view where a branch and a leaf are distinguishable. Dragging a parent object produces `[object Object]` in the result.

**A node reporting success is not the outcome happening.** The Gmail node sent correctly and the mail was in Sent — it had landed in spam and was never received. n8n is telling the truth about its own node; delivery is somebody else's system.

**Revoking an OAuth grant silently breaks the workflow.** Every grant is visible and deletable under Overview → Credentials, but a workflow configured against a deleted credential stops working.

ops.title: Build 2 — IF for spam, Sheets for the log

ops.label: n8n Form trigger
ops.detail: Unchanged from Build 1. Everything from Build 1 stays; one node is inserted and one is appended.

ops.label: Basic LLM Chain — summarise, and append a tag
ops.detail: The chain's output is free text and the IF needs something testable, so the prompt is made to append a tag at the end of the text. Simplest thought process available: the IF node has a text contains operator, so give it a word to find. Five rounds of prompt iteration to get there — see the prompt iteration table.

ops.label: IF: chain text contains "booking"
ops.detail:
Goes after the chain, because the IF has to test the chain's output — put it before and you are testing raw form text, which is what the chain was for. Insert it by hovering the connection between two nodes and clicking add, not delete: the node lands in the middle of the existing edge.

Why not a keyword list instead of an LLM: you cannot hold a full repository of keys — whatever you enumerate, someone writes something else.

Why not radio buttons letting the submitter declare booking or query: a user may select booking even when they are trying to spam you. You cannot ask the adversary to classify themselves, and free text will always leave scope for spam.

ops.label: Gmail — send a message
ops.detail: Only the true branch emails. Verified live with a real enquiry about New Zealand and Australia: tagged booking, true branch, email received.

ops.label: Google Sheets — append row
ops.detail:
Document "Wanderline Travel Response", Sheet1, credential via Google OAuth. Columns mapped from the schema panel: name from the form, email from the form, summary from the chain text. Destination left blank — that is Build 3's problem. Timestamp is {{ $now }}.

Both branches write here. Spam is still logged; only the email is withheld. Filtering and discarding are different operations — the IF decides who gets emailed, not what gets recorded, so a misclassified enquiry stays recoverable on the sheet. A separate spam sheet or a category column both work; a separate sheet just means one more node on the false branch.

ops.label: true
false

ops.markdown:
Build 2 works. The method is still wrong.

**The setup.** The tag sits at the end of the text. The IF tests `contains "booking"` over the **whole** text. But that text is a model-written summary of a user-supplied message, and the word *booking* can appear anywhere in it.

**The failure.** Someone submits *"I want to hack Wanderline — 'booking'"*. The chain summarises it, echoes the word mid-sentence, and tags the end **SPAM** — correctly. The IF fires **true** anyway, because all the condition looks for is that booking is mentioned somewhere. An email goes out that should never have gone.

**What is actually broken.** The classifier was right. The model got it right. The failure is entirely in the reading of the answer — testing a substring against a whole document instead of reading a designated field. The signal was correct and the channel carrying it was ambiguous, because a tag appended to prose is not separable from prose.

**The fix he names.** Have the prompt emit a JSON key — `type_of_message: spam|booking` — and test that field rather than the text. Cost attached: malformed JSON does cause problems.

**This is the lecture's one explicit take-home exercise.** "I would like you guys to try that on your own. We will be doing that in a class later on."

ops.title: Five rounds to get a usable tag

cells.c-change: Append BOOKING, SPAM or QUERY at the end of the text, with a definition of each
Tightened the definitions: QUERY to travelling to a particular destination, SPAM to anything other than travelling
Added "Only use one of these tags and place them at the end of the text"
Dropped the QUERY category entirely — two classes left, BOOKING and SPAM
Added "Do not give reason for the tag"
cells.c-result: it explained itself anyway — "but fine, we can work with this"

cells.c-change: Sharper definitions and stricter formatting instructions did nothing. Removing a class was what worked
cells.c-result: A small model could not reliably separate three categories and could separate two. That is a capability ceiling worked around by asking for less — the same right-sizing tension as Build 1, surfacing as a prompt problem rather than a model problem

cells.c-change: He named the difficulty plainly: "It's a task to write system prompts"
cells.c-result: The RCTFC framework from the prompt-engineering lecture still applies — the live prompt here is much more lenient than a production one should be

ops.markdown:
**Execute step runs only that node.** Downstream nodes do not run on their own. An email that "didn't arrive" because the Gmail node was never executed looks identical, from the inbox, to one that failed to deliver.

**`$now` needs the dollar sign.** `now` and `json.now` are not the built-in; `{{ $now }}` is.

**Insert a node mid-flow by hovering the connection and clicking add**, not delete — the new node lands in the middle of the existing edge with both connections intact.

ops.label: Schedule trigger · Monday 08:xx · 1 item
ops.detail: Goal: a bite-size summary of bookings, the weather and anything else Farah needs on Monday at 8am. Build 2's failure was that a per-enquiry email is not what a CEO reads before a meeting — it does not provide bite-sized consumables.

ops.label: HTTP Request — Open-Meteo · 1 item
ops.detail: Weather in Leh, Ladakh. Sits here, before Get rows, for a reason that only becomes visible in the next section: node order is what decides how many times this call is made.

ops.label: Google Sheets: get rows · n items
ops.detail:
Same document and sheet that Builds 1 and 2 write to. The sheet is the interface between the two workflows — Build 3 is a new workflow reading what the first one recorded, not an extension of it.

Executing it returns every row as its own item. Not one item containing n rows: n items. Every node downstream runs once per incoming item, which is the entire cause of the duplicate-run bug in the next section.

ops.label: Aggregate · n items into 1
ops.detail: Introduced later in the build, once the duplicate-run problem has been diagnosed.

ops.label: Basic LLM Chain · 1 call
ops.detail: Writes the brief from the aggregated rows plus the weather.

ops.label: Gmail — send a message · 1 email

ops.markdown:
A clearly non-travel submission — *"I'm going to work, I want to earn more money"* — came back tagged **booking**. Twice.

**The attribution is the lesson.** "This is a fault on my system prompt side and not the message side." The input was not ambiguous; the prompt was underspecified. The tempting wrong move is sitting right there — blame the strange input.

**The fix.** A saved prompt ending: *"Then on a new final line, write exactly one word: booking if they want to book, general if it is a question, or spam if it is junk."* It returned `general`. The IF was changed to match the lowercase word.

**Read against the five rounds in Build 2.** This reinstates a third category — the one that had to be dropped to get a correct tag at all. What makes it work now is that the *output format* is pinned (a new final line, exactly one word) rather than the category definitions being elaborated further. Asking for less and asking more precisely are both live moves, and this is a refinement of that earlier lesson rather than a contradiction of it.

**What is still not fixed.** The tag still sits at the end of the text and the IF still matches a word inside it. The substring false positive is tightened, not closed — the JSON-key exercise still stands.

A student suggested **meta-prompting** for this specific model. Agreed: that would help the most here.

cells.c-detail: Seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, and custom (cron)

He googled "cron expression for once a year on 5th July", got 0 0 5 7 * and pasted it — then said he would not recommend relying on that. Use the picker where the picker can express the schedule; cron is the escape hatch for what it cannot, and an unverified pasted expression is a scheduled bug
Weeks, every 1 week, Monday, hour 8, plus a minute value — set through the picker, not cron

Meeting at 9, report at 8. "It does not have to wait for a human interaction" — the brief is generated while nobody is awake to ask for it. The same insight as the 3am enquiries, applied to the output side instead of the input side
Birthday offers on a yearly cron — raised by a student and confirmed

ops.title: Calling an HTTP API from a workflow

ops.label: Find an API and read its docs
ops.detail: Searched "API for weather" and picked Open-Meteo — free, no authentication. Its docs page offers a ready-made curl request.

ops.label: Paste the curl into Postman's URL box
ops.detail: Postman parses a pasted curl into URL plus query parameters, laid out separately. You now have a working request you can edit before any of it touches the workflow.

ops.label: Test it with your real values first
ops.detail: Found Leh, Ladakh's latitude and longitude (34.209…, 77.6…), swapped them in, ran it again: 6.7 °C, wind 2.8. The request is proven before it becomes a node — so you are never debugging an API call and a workflow at the same time.

ops.label: Translate it into the HTTP Request node
ops.detail:
Method GET. URL is only the part before the ? — the bare endpoint. Then tick Send query parameters and add latitude, longitude and current as separate entries.

"Your immediate thought would be copy this entire request … it may work, but this is asking only for the URL." The node has a structured place for parameters because they are then individually editable, individually expressible, and visible as data rather than buried in a string.

ops.label: Ask for the field you actually want
ops.detail:
The current parameter is required to get a temperature at all — without it the response carries latitude, longitude, elevation and nothing else. Value used: temperature_2m (wind_speed_10m was dropped).

Correction to what was said live: 2m is the measurement height — temperature at 2 metres above ground, the meteorological standard — not a two-minute refresh rate. The freshness claim happens to be true; the mechanism given for it is not. Carry the parameter name, not the explanation.

ops.markdown:
**The unit of data is the item, not the payload.** A node does not receive "the data" — it receives a queue, and **it executes once per entry**.

Get Rows on a sheet with fifty rows hands you "50 rows in individual boxes", not "50 rows in one box". Each box then runs the chain, and the email.

**How it surfaced.** Executing the HTTP node ran it twice. Two rows upstream, two items, two executions.

### Consequence one — node order decides call count

Moving the HTTP request **before** Get Rows, directly after the trigger, calls the API once, because the trigger emits one item. This is not diagram tidiness: an API call placed downstream of a multi-item node multiplies requests by the row count, and on a paid API that is a bill.

### Consequence two — Aggregate

Get Rows still emits n items, so anything after it still runs n times. **Aggregate** sits between Get Rows and the chain with the option *all item data into a single list*, and collapses n items into 1.

Its funnel icon is the mnemonic, and its limit is explicit: it converts multiple rows into one dataset, **it will not summarize**. A structural operation, not a semantic one — contents unchanged. Demonstrated at 2 rows, then again after adding a third: Get Rows gives 3 items, Aggregate still gives 1.

### Why not parallel branches

A student asked whether HTTP and Sheets could run as parallel branches. Possible — but "then you'll have two triggers going forward". One straight line ensures there are none, and branching creates a merge problem you then have to solve.

ops.detail: Option: all item data into a single list. Collapses the n items from Get rows into 1, so the chain is called once and one email goes out. Structural, not semantic — it fans in, it does not summarise. Inserted only after the duplicate-email bug had been seen live.

ops.title: Reading the canvas, and the chain's errors

cells.c-err: Green border, red border, a triangle
cells.c-means: Green: the node ran. Red: it failed. A triangle: a configuration problem — something unset, as distinct from something that ran and broke
cells.c-do: Read the canvas before opening anything

cells.c-err: "A model sub-node must be connected and enabled"
cells.c-means: "It knows what the prompt is. It does not know who to ask that prompt to." The chain node is a socket; the model is a separate sub-node

cells.c-err: "The service is receiving too many requests from you"
cells.c-means: Two different causes behind one message: too many requests per minute, or the token cap. Here the error body showed output tokens per minute at the tier limit — the prompt plus expected output was over the cap, not the request count
cells.c-do: Read the error body to tell which. A token-cap breach is a tier or model problem, not a pacing problem

cells.c-err: A model that returns nothing usable
cells.c-means: Wrong kind of model. A prompt-guard model from the same list is a classifier, not a chat model — the dropdown lists everything the provider hosts, and not everything hosted answers prompts
cells.c-do: Pick a chat model. Model names as heard in the lecture are unverified, so check the provider's own listing

cells.c-err: The rule under all of it
cells.c-means: "If the error is something related to the model, then the model needs to change. If you sit here on the basic LLM chain and keep making changes, nothing will change"
cells.c-do: Fiddling with the node that reports an error is the default instinct and it is often the wrong node

ops.markdown:
Two rows of real data in the sheet. The small model reported, in sequence:

- "100+ bookings made, focused on Australia"
- then "total bookings 50"
- then "[name] made five bookings"
- and "average temperature 15–20°" when the API had returned 6.5

"This has hallucinated to the very ends of the world."

**The part that matters.** Adding *"Strictly use data given below. Don't make your own numbers or hallucinate"* did not help. **A prompt instruction cannot add a capability the model lacks** — "don't hallucinate" works on a model that could have been grounded anyway; on one that cannot, it is decoration.

Switching to a stronger model on the same provider produced a grounded answer immediately. "The cheaper the model, the more hallucination it provides you."

**Why the earlier choice came due here.** Picking a small model for a simple request was defensible in Build 1. The task stopped being simple when it became synthesis over retrieved data rather than summarisation of one message. Counting two rows and not inventing a number is a capability, not a phrasing.

**The accident worth keeping.** The stronger model, being grounded, honestly reported the temperature as *missing* — which exposed the next bug. The weak model had been papering over a real data failure with a plausible number. Upgrading did not only fix the output; it surfaced a defect that was already there.

ops.value: It came due in Build 3: the small model fabricated booking counts and a temperature from two rows of real data, and a "do not hallucinate" instruction did not save it. "Simple task" is a judgement you can get wrong, and the symptom surfaces two builds later as wrong content in an email

ops.markdown:
One symptom, **two different causes** — both seen in the same build.

**Cause one: a parent dragged instead of a leaf.** The temperature expression pointed at the `current` object rather than the `temperature_2m` leaf inside it. Fix: drag the leaf. Schema view is the only view where a branch and a leaf are distinguishable.

**Cause two: a collection forced into a string.** The chain's prompt was pointed at the Aggregate node's `data` — an array of objects dropped into a text field, which has no string form. Fix: serialise it.

```
{{ JSON.stringify($json.data, null, 2) }}
```

Pasted in, the prompt preview listed all three rows in full.

### The method, taught explicitly

Screenshot the node. Open a **temporary** chat — "I don't want to save it in my history". Describe the situation in one line. Ask for a "small answer".

His own framing: "Do you need to remember that? Not necessarily … ChatGPT is always going to help to get small quick functions."

**What is worth holding is the symptom, not the incantation.** `[object Object]` means a shape problem: either a parent where a leaf was meant, or a collection where a string was meant. Knowing which of the two you are looking at is the skill; the exact function is lookup.

**Result after both fixes:** "two bookings were made … one general query … Ladakh temperature is 6.5 °C" — one LLM call, one email.

The working email was a wall of text. The fix went into the **system prompt**, not the Gmail node.

A **Format** section was added:

> The response should only contain the email body: Hello Farah, hope you're doing well, below is the morning bite before your 8 AM call. Booking details: <summary>. Ladakh temperature: <value>. Best, <name>.

**Two things are doing work there.** The template, and the constraint *only contain the email body* — without it the model prefaces its output with "Here's the email I've drafted for you", and that goes out to the CEO. Pinning what the output must **not** contain is as much of the job as pinning what it must.

**Why the prompt and not the transport node.** The chain already produces the text; Gmail only carries it. Formatting in Gmail would mean reassembling a string from pieces the model had already assembled once. One place owns the output, and it is the place that generated it.

**Three practical notes**

- A literal `\n` appearing in the body needs handling at the expression level — a model writing an escape sequence into its text is not the same as a newline.
- HTML in the body is possible.
- A tabular summary (metric / value) came from adding one sentence: *"lastly, here is a tabular summary"*. Nothing structural — the model produces the table.

Why call a weather API at all — why not just ask the model for the temperature?

**Two arguments, and they are different.**

It hallucinates, and it does so confidently. The model says Jaipur is 20 °C, you pack a thin shirt, it is 35 °C. "It will confidently tell me that this is the temperature whereas it is not." The failure is not that it does not know — it is that not knowing and knowing look identical in the output.

And even when it is not hallucinating, it is answering from a snapshot. An API updates on a short cycle; a model's number is at best whatever its training data held. On a trek, hours out would be massive.

### The rule

> **Use the LLM for what only an LLM can do** — summarising English, generating an email, creative content. If something else can do it faster, cheaper and more authoritatively, use that instead.

**Three criteria, and they fail differently.** *Faster* is latency. *Cheaper* is cost per call. **Authoritative is the one that decides** — an API is the source of record for the temperature in a way no model can be, however good models get. The first two are optimisations; the third is a correctness argument.

**This resolves the tension running through the lecture.** Build 1 said do not overkill with an expensive model. Build 3 said the cheap model hallucinates, use a better one. This says the real move is not to ask the model at all when something else owns the answer. Right-sizing applies only to work that genuinely needs a model — and a good deal of what gets put in an LLM node is a lookup wearing a costume.

ops.label: Know which part is fixed and which is live
ops.detail:
The location is hard-coded — Ladakh's coordinates sit in the query parameters. The value is not: "tomorrow if I run this workflow, the temperature will not be 6.5." Every run fetches fresh.

To make the location dynamic, chain a geocoding request first: city name in, latitude and longitude out, fed into the weather request. The pattern generalises — an API that wants an identifier you do not have usually has a companion API that resolves it.

Goal: a bite-size summary of bookings, the weather and anything else Farah needs on Monday at 8am. Build 2's failure was that a per-enquiry email is not what a CEO reads before a meeting — it does not provide bite-sized consumables.

What Build 3 actually added, in his own summary: "two new things: first is an HTTP request and how we make that work; second is aggregation of rows to get a summary out of it." The biggest-looking build of the three contributed two nodes. Everything else was configuration and bugs — which is the realistic ratio, and the build principle restated.

ops.title: Error handling — three settings and a safety net

cells.c-does: The first three are in a node's Settings tab, which most people never open. The fourth is in Workflow Settings
cells.c-when: None of these is a node you drag onto the canvas — they are checkboxes on nodes you already have, which is why they stay invisible

cells.c-does: Re-attempts up to Max Tries, waiting Wait Between Tries milliseconds each time. Demonstrated on the HTTP node: fails, tries again, stops on the last attempt
cells.c-when: The node calls an outside service. Networks blip and APIs rate-limit, and most failures succeed on attempt two. The specific values shown live are unverified — the mechanism is the point, not the numbers

cells.c-does: Adds a second, red output. Failed items go down it instead of killing the run
cells.c-when: One bad item should not stop the other eleven. "Stopping the workflow is an overkill" — the brief goes out without the temperature

cells.c-does: Passes the failure response forward as data — "server unavailable" arrives on the error branch as something you can read and act on
cells.c-when: You want the failure answered rather than just survived. Demonstrated: the error branch calls a different weather API and rejoins the main line at Get rows — a fallback path built from the same kind of nodes as the happy path

cells.c-does: Emits an empty item instead of nothing, so downstream nodes still run
cells.c-when: A lookup legitimately finds nothing and you still want the found-nothing path to run. A sheet query matching no rows is not an error, but it emits nothing, and nothing means no downstream execution — so the "no bookings this week" email never sends

cells.c-does: Glossed live as "even if it's an error, we send it forward". That is not what it does
cells.c-when: The printed reference is right and the live gloss is wrong: it covers a node that succeeds and legitimately returns nothing, which is a different case from error handling. The gloss conflates it with Continue (using error output)

cells.c-does: A separate workflow, started by an Error Trigger, that runs whenever this one dies
cells.c-when: Always, on anything running unattended. "This is what makes failure visible"

ops.title: Degraded output is a design decision

ops.markdown:
**"Stopping the workflow is an overkill."** The bookings summary matters more than the weather; Farah can check her phone for the temperature. So the failed weather call goes down the error output and the brief goes out without it.

**Generalised:** error handling is not making nothing fail. It is deciding, per node, what the **degraded** version of your output looks like and whether it is still worth sending.

A brief with bookings and no weather is useful. No brief is not. That judgement is a product decision, not a technical one, and it has to be made node by node — which is why the settings are per node rather than per workflow.

**The different case: Error Workflow.** Everything above handles failure *inside* the flow. A separate workflow on an Error Trigger handles the case where the flow itself is gone — "this is what makes failure visible".

Without it an unattended workflow fails silently, and you find out when somebody asks why they stopped getting the Monday brief. It is the same shape as the unpublished workflow and the email sitting in spam: the system reports nothing wrong, because there is nothing there to do the reporting.

ops.label: Debugging a workflow
ops.detail: "Debugging" was on the whiteboard agenda with no section of its own — it was taught by doing. These are the moves gathered from across the three builds. Only one of the nine is genuinely tool-specific, and even that is a JavaScript fact wearing an n8n hat.

ops.label: Read what the system is already telling you
Configure against real sample data — and re-run the trigger after editing it
ops.detail: Run the trigger once so downstream nodes are built against output you can see. Edit the trigger afterwards and the sample goes stale while still looking valid.

ops.label: Read the border colours
ops.detail: Green ran. Red failed. A triangle means misconfigured — something unset, as distinct from something that ran and broke.

ops.label: Read the error body and fix the node it names
ops.detail: A rate-limit error belongs to the model sub-node, not the chain that reported it. Fiddling with the node showing the error is the default instinct and often the wrong node.

ops.label: Count the items
ops.detail: A node that ran twice was handed two items. Reorder so single-item work happens before the fan-out, and Aggregate to fan back in.

ops.label: Your workflow is not the only system involved
Step-executed nodes do not run downstream nodes
ops.detail: The "missing" email had simply not been sent yet. From the inbox this is indistinguishable from a delivery failure.

ops.label: Check spam before blaming the workflow
ops.detail: The Gmail node sent correctly and the mail was in Sent. It had been filtered on the way in.

ops.label: You may be debugging the wrong layer
Before rewriting the prompt a fourth time, try a better model
ops.detail: Small models misclassify and invent numbers. A prompt instruction cannot add a capability the model lacks — three rounds of rewording is a signal that you are against a ceiling, not an ambiguity.

ops.label: Do not hoard syntax
[object Object] means a parent dragged instead of a leaf, or an array passed into a string
ops.detail: Drag the leaf, or JSON.stringify(...). Recognising which of the two cases you are in is the skill; the exact function is lookup.

ops.label: Screenshot, temporary chat, ask for a small answer
ops.detail: "Do you need to remember that? Not necessarily." A temporary chat keeps it out of history; one line of description and a request for a short answer gets the expression back.
